implementation_notes: The standard library ships the reusable barrier directly: threading.Barrier(parties, action=None, timeout=None) blocks wait() until all parties arrive, resets itself for the next generation, runs the optional action once when the barrier is released, and returns a unique arrival index (0..parties-1). wait(timeout) raises BrokenBarrierError when the barrier is broken or reset while waiting; abort() breaks it deliberately and reset() re-arms it - which is precisely the failure policy a barrier needs. The one-shot latch has no dedicated class: threading.Event plus a counter covers latency fan-in, and a Barrier used by all producers covers the join-style case.
pitfalls: An exception anywhere in a party (or an abort) breaks the barrier: every waiting thread raises BrokenBarrierError, and the barrier stays broken until reset() - catch it and convert it into the group's failure, never into a retry loop.
In CPython the GIL means a barrier in thread-based code synchronizes well but does not make CPU-bound phases parallel; use processes (multiprocessing.Barrier has the same API) for real parallel work.
The optional action runs inside the barrier's release path, in one of the parties' threads: blocking or raising there breaks the barrier for everyone and serializes the phase.

variants.name: asyncio.Barrier (3.11+) with gather-based fan-in
variants.idiom_name: asyncio.Barrier + await wait(); asyncio.gather / TaskGroup for the latch
variants.implementation_notes: Blocking is forbidden in asyncio - threading.Barrier.wait() would stall the event loop - so the library added asyncio.Barrier in 3.11: await barrier.wait() rendezvous with the same parties semantics, and await abort()/reset() (or the broken state) provides the failure path. For the one-shot fan-in, asyncio.gather(* awaitables) already joins every task and propagates the first exception, and asyncio.TaskGroup (3.11+) gives structured concurrency with cancellation on failure; a hand-rolled asyncio.Event counter is only needed when completions arrive from callbacks rather than awaitables.
variants.code_sketch:
import asyncio

phase = asyncio.Barrier(parties=n)          # Python 3.11+

async def worker(i: int) -> None:
    for step in range(steps):
        await compute(i, step)
        await phase.wait()                  # never blocks the event loop
        ...
# one-shot fan-in:
results = await asyncio.gather(*(process(s) for s in shards))
pitfalls: threading.Barrier.wait() inside a coroutine blocks the whole loop; only asyncio.Barrier (3.11+) is awaitable, so older interpreters need an Event/counter composition or a thread hop.

Aborting an asyncio barrier raises asyncio.BrokenBarrierError in every waiter, and a task that dies before waiting leaves the rest blocked - structured concurrency (TaskGroup) is what makes the cancellation travel, a bare gather does not cancel siblings.
asyncio.gather without return_exceptions propagates the first exception while the other tasks keep running; cancel them explicitly if the fan-in is meant to be all-or-nothing.
